title: The Mission

What could a working day in my chosen role involve?
This is an imagined working day.

stages.title: Arrival task
body: What is your chosen role? Name one task.
What is a shift?
You cannot use the coffee machine safely yet. What do you do?
What is missing from a blog with no times?
BLUE / GREEN / AMBER / RED. Choose a reset if needed.
stages.notes: 4 minutes. Regulation: BLUE low energy; GREEN ready; AMBER tense; RED overwhelmed. Offer water, quiet breathing, a brief pause or a quieter seat. Do not require a public colour disclosure. Privately agree the first return action and keep access to the task. Expected answers: the learner’s own selected role and a relevant task; a planned period of work; stop and ask a trained adult, do not use unfamiliar equipment; a clear order or sense of when tasks happen. No machine use is required. Read or rephrase and accept pointing. No cold calling or pair work. Use individual stations and a private check-in. Read, rephrase or scribe the learner’s own words; record support. Do not supply the learner’s assessed choice or explanation. Offer a quiet reset, then one clear return step. Only VF, WS, I, NS, E and R are used; confirm local code definitions before marking. E does not establish an award claim.

stages.title: An imagined café shift
body: My shift starts at 7.
First, I check the work area with my supervisor.
At lunchtime, I help take orders.
Before I finish, I tidy my station.
Which words show the order?
stages.notes: 2 minutes. Read the four-line classroom model aloud. Times and duties are invented examples, not a claim about a real business or learner. Expected time/order words: starts at 7, first, at lunchtime, before I finish. Connect the blog to the role and a reader who needs to follow the day.

stages.title: Today I can
body: Produce a blog describing what you would expect to do in a normal working day in your chosen role.
I can put job tasks in order.
I can use times or time phrases.
I can explain the hardest part.
stages.notes: Untimed. Read the exact supplied outcome. [QUAL] — planner mapping. The learner criteria are classroom success checks, not quotations from the official student book.

stages.title: From timeline to a sentence
body: 7:00 start: check my station.
9:00 task: check orders.
12:00 task: help serve lunch.
14:00 task: tidy and restock.
15:00 end: hand over to the next worker.
At __, I would __.
stages.notes: 5 minutes. Model an imagined café-assistant shift. Use five ordered entries: start, three tasks, end. Turn one line into a sentence and explain the words “I would” mark a hypothetical day. Times are classroom examples, not prescribed employment hours for a young person. No actual work placement or duties are being assigned. Hinge: an entry says 15:00 before 9:00. What needs changing? Expected put the tasks in time order.

stages.title: A receptionist timeline
body: Choose a start time and an end time.
Between them: check bookings, welcome a guest, pass on a message.
Put the tasks in a sensible order.
First I would __. Later I would __.
stages.notes: 5 minutes. Build one imagined receptionist timeline on the board through optional pointing or short private contributions. Adults supply the worked-model role; learners still choose their own timeline later. Hinge: the blog says “I work hard all day” but gives no tasks. Is the working day clear? Expected no, include specific tasks and order. Do not require whole-class performance.

stages.title: Your working-day blog
body: Use the job role you chose.
Plan a start, three tasks and an end.
Write five sentences, type them or explain a photo sequence.
Use times or time phrases.
At __, I would __.
Supported: Order the cards, then use the five sentence frames.
Independent: Write five linked sentences from your timeline.
Aspire: Add a shift problem and explain your response.
stages.notes: 12 minutes. First part of the 18-minute individual task. Offer the role cards, blank timeline and blog frame. A learner may record their own words for adult transcription, clearly marked as scribed. A photo sequence must be explained by the learner; generic stock images alone do not show their understanding. No public posting or account is needed.

route_tasks.Supported: Order the prompt cards, then use the five sentence starters. Dictate if needed.
route_tasks.Independent: Write your own five linked sentences from your timeline.
route_tasks.Aspire: Add a realistic problem during the shift and explain what you would do.

stages.title: Your evidence
body: Add: The hardest part would be __ because __.
Check your role, task order and time words.
Keep your timeline with your blog or transcript.
Label VOC1-L2-E1.
Supported: Find the start and end. Read your reason privately.
Independent: Match each timeline task to your blog.
Aspire: Explain why your problem response would help.
stages.notes: 6 minutes. Complete the 18-minute You Do. Keep actual dates, file references and support entries blank until the learner’s work exists. Listen to the learner explain one event to establish ownership. A hypothetical role blog must not be copied into a CV as real employment or claimed skill experience.

route_tasks.Supported: Point to the start and end. Read your hardest-part line with an adult.
route_tasks.Independent: Check that each timeline task appears in your blog.
route_tasks.Aspire: Explain how your response to a problem would protect service or safety.

stages.title: Tidy and file
body: Save or print your work with your name or learner code.
File the timeline and blog together.
A transcript uses your own words and is marked as scribed.
I improved __.
stages.notes: 4 minutes. Use an approved offline document or school system; no public upload is required. Save the actual work reference in the evidence app. Check the learner identifier and date. Record real active minutes and support under the workbook’s signed-Plan rule. Do not add the separate Careers lesson to hospitality hours. Do not automatically mark the mapped challenge achieved.

stages.title: Exit ticket
body: Read, say or point to one sentence in your blog.
What happens at that point in the shift?
At __, I would __.
stages.notes: 2 minutes. Private adult check. If speech is difficult, the learner can point and the adult can read their sentence back for confirmation. Check that the selected event fits the chosen role. Carry the chosen target role into Careers, but only truthful real experience belongs in a CV.

support_pages.title: Timeline and blog model
lines: Worked example only. This imagined shift is not your work history.
7:00 start — check the station with my supervisor.
9:00 task — check orders.
12:00 task — help serve lunch.
14:00 task — tidy and restock.
15:00 end — hand over.

My imagined shift starts at 7. First, I would check my station with my supervisor. At 9, I would check orders. At lunchtime, I would help serve customers. Before I finish at 3, I would tidy and hand over.
The hardest part would be keeping orders correct because several customers might ask at once.

support_pages.title: Order and choose prompts
lines: Supported / MCQ: choose your role, then put these labels in order: start / first task / next task / later task / end.
Sentence frames: My shift would start at __. First, I would __. At __, I would __. Later, I would __. Before I finish at __, I would __.
Reason frame: The hardest part would be __ because __.
Independent: use your own wording and check it against your timeline.
Aspire: add a problem, your response and a reason.
If none of the model tasks fits your role, ask for the role card or use a different sensible task.

support_pages.title: Role task prompts
lines: Receptionist: check bookings; welcome guests; pass on messages; hand over.
Housekeeper: check the room list; prepare rooms; report a missing item; hand over.
Café assistant: check the station; take orders; serve the correct order; tidy.
Chef: check the menu and ingredients; prepare a dish; check the order; clean safely.
Kitchen porter: check safe instructions; clean equipment; return items; tidy.
These are classroom prompts. Actual duties vary and training is needed.

planner_sections.heading: Teaching and answers
paragraphs: Arrival: selected role and sensible task; shift means a planned work period; ask a trained adult rather than use unfamiliar equipment; time words make the day followable. The four-line starter is an imagined café-assistant day.

Model start, three tasks and end. The receptionist We Do uses checking bookings, welcoming guests and passing on a message. Hinge: a general “work hard” statement lacks specific tasks; a reversed timeline needs reordering.

paragraphs: Supported: order cards and sentence frames, with dictation where needed. MCQ access: select and order labels then add role-specific tasks. Independent: own wording. Aspire: add a plausible problem, action and reason.

Keep the focus on a clear sequence rather than a minimum decorative layout. Read one sentence back to the learner and invite a single improvement. Regulation: BLUE low energy; GREEN ready; AMBER tense; RED overwhelmed. Offer water, quiet breathing, a brief pause or a quieter seat. Do not require a public colour disclosure. Privately agree the first return action and keep access to the task.

No cold calling or pair work. Use individual stations and a private check-in. Read, rephrase or scribe the learner’s own words; record support. Do not supply the learner’s assessed choice or explanation. Offer a quiet reset, then one clear return step. Only VF, WS, I, NS, E and R are used; confirm local code definitions before marking. E does not establish an award claim.

planner_sections.heading: Lundy and Careers link
paragraphs: Space: individual station. Voice: learner chooses a role and events. Audience: adult listens to one selected sentence. Influence: the learner improves an unclear event.

Carry the chosen target job into the CV lesson. The source links the blog to CV lines, but an imagined shift is not proof of real experience. Use the blog for role insight only. Any CV skill or experience needs a true example from the learner’s own activity.

planner_sections.heading: Minutes and filing
paragraphs: Planned hospitality time is 40 minutes. Actual date, actual active minutes, work reference, support and adult initials remain blank until taught. Follow the workbook’s signed-Plan rule. Do not count the separate Careers lesson. Store the real work reference in the evidence app. [VERIFY] Official programme hours/credit rule before any claim.

staff_answers: Shift = a planned period of work. A timeline shows events in order. Accept times such as 7:00 or phrases such as first, at lunchtime and before I finish.

The starter’s order words are starts at 7, first, at lunchtime and before I finish. Its four lines are a model; the independent output asks for five sentences or an explained sequence plus a hardest-part line.
Possible receptionist model: start and check bookings; welcome a guest; check a request; pass on a message; end with handover. Many sensible sequences are possible.

A hardest-part reason should connect to a duty: keeping orders correct because several people may ask at once. A plausible response might be repeat the order or ask the supervisor. Do not require the learner to claim they have already done this.

Completion check: role, start/three tasks/end, order, time words, five sentences or explained sequence, hardest-part reason, date/ownership/support. Exact official student-book criterion remains [VERIFY].
